\ssyrian Deeds and Documents Recording the Transfer of Property ncluding the so-called private contracts, legal decisions and proclamations preserved in the Kouyunjik Collections of the British Museum Chiefly of the 7th Century B.C. COP/ED, COLLATED, ARRANGED, ABSTRACTED,
BY The Rev. C. H. W. JOHNS M.A.

THE DUKE OF DEVONSHIRE, K.G, LORD PRESIDENT OF HER MAJESTV's MOST HONOURABLE PRIVY COUNCIL, AND CHANCELLOR OK THE UNIVERSITY OF CAMBRIDGE,

THE texts here published, most of them for the first time, were all copied directly from the original tablets in the British Museum. The copying, collation, arrangement and autography of the texts has occupied the leisure of some three years. The well known costliness of publication in the case of similar undertakings would have indefinitely postponed the appearance of this work, had not the generosity of the Dukes of Devonshire and Portland relieved me of the heavy financial responsibility. To them 1 publicly :ender here my grateful acknowledgement. What gain to knowledge this work shall confer, is their gift to the world. The interest which my old master in Assyrian Studies, Professor S. A. Strong, took in what I was doing not only encouraged me to continue but opened for me the door to publicity. May what I have done bring him something of the only reward a master has at the hands of a pupil. To Dr E. A. W. Budge, Keeper of the Department of Egyptian and Assyrian Antiquities in the British Museum, are offered my sincerest thanks for every facility that a student could desire. To Mr L. W. King I am indebted for many friendly hints and much valued advice. The kindness received from all these gentlemen is a pleasure to recall and apart from the interest of the work would have been sufficient inducement to persevere. The interest of the work to me was intense. Merely to handle what Sargon or Sennacherib had written, or read or held in his hand repays the labour needful to learn Cuneiform. The purpose with which this enterprise started was to obtain light, if possible, on some of the obscure historical questions of the Old Testament. That obscurity is due directly, in some cases, to the contributions of Assyriology to history. It has been suggested that some historical inscriptions may shew bias, the deeds of sale are surely free from such suspicion. Moreover they are absolutely contemporary with

the events they record. Long ago Geo. Smith in "The Assyrian Canon " shewed the value of this class of documents for chronology, and his work suggested the idea that were a complete series of dated documents available, a proof or disproof might be found of the theory of gaps in the Eponym Canon. No one however could tell how complete the series preserved in the British Museum might be until the tablets had been examined one by one. Further, rich material for the study of the popular side of Assyrian Religion was likely to be furnished by the enormous number of proper names these texts contain. There was even a vague hope of settling the value of some ancient Hebrew traditions (e.g. the use of Adrammelech both as the name of a god and of Sennacherib's murderer). On all sides were ever exciting possibilities of discovery. The texts included in this volume have chiefly to do with negotiations for the transfer of property, being for the most part deeds of sale, loans or advances of money or goods, leases of property, etc. In the "Catalogue of the Cuneiform Tablets in the Kouyunjik Collection of the British Museum " they are generally entered as "private contracts," "legal decisions" or "proclamations." It is however very difficult to construct a title that shall suit them all. Indeed they are not all essentially of the same nature. The loans or advances seem to have been made by a landlord or his steward to tenants or servants to meet current expenses. The sales effected seem nearly always to have been to some high placed official as buyer (very often on behalf of the King, the Crown-prince, or the QueenMother). In this and other respects these texts differ widely from the trade documents published by Strassmaier. These are scarcely ' private ' documents in that the purchases were for the Court. Still less is the term ' contract ' generally appropriate. The document, it is true, constituted a binding agreement but it was certainly not a "legal decision." The latter term must surely be confined to documents embodying the ruling of some judicial functionary upon a case submitted to him. The term 'proclamation' again would equally well describe a very different class of document from those to which it is applied. They are decrees of a sovereign conferring certam privileges upon and assigning certain property to some official, presumably as a reward for distinguished services. A fuller discussion of the nomenclature of this class of documents is reserved for the second volume. The lack of definite terms must however be painfully felt by any one using the Catalogue. It would

be impossible to make from it a list which should contain all the texts of one sort without at the same time including others of a completely different kind. " Private contract," " legal decision " and " proclamation " seem used interchangeably. As a consequence when all the tablets entered under the head of " private contracts " had been copied, it was clearly unreasonable to exclude the rest of the "legal decisions and proclamations." Further, when all the tablets entered under the three heads were arranged and classified ; it soon became clear that many of them had been improperly included. With these it then seemed desirable to class other tablets of like character, entered under various other headings. Even some socalled "historical inscriptions" proved on examination to be fragments of others called " proclamations." This statement of facts is not meant to reflect any discredit on the respected compiler of the Catalogue, who could not be expected to revise the nomenclature already in use nor to fix arbitrarily and without discussion the limits of each term. Some such explanation is however needed to account for the necessarily incomplete nature of this collection of texts. Supposing it to contain the texts of all the tablets entered in the Catalogue under certain headings, there is yet little security that no similar tablets have been omitted, since they may have been disguised by apparently unrelated titles. Still this collection is as correct and complete as my understanding of the Catalogue has allowed me to make it. The " private contract," so called, of Assyria has long been known to Assyriologists. Thirty-six were published in the Third Volume of the Cuneiform Inscriptions of Western Asia in 1870. J. Oppert and J. Menant gave eight more in transcription and translation in their Documents juridiques de V Assyrie et de la Chaldk (Paris 1877). Mr T. G. Pinches furnished the texts of twelve more for the Corpus Inscriptiofiu/n Semiticarum (Pars 11. Tom. i. fasc. i. Paris 1889). Dr F. E. Peiser in vol. iv. of Schrader's Keilinschriftliche Bibliothek (Berlin 1896) gave a transcription and translation of thirty more. Dr C. Bezold, Dr J. A. Craig, Dr R. Briinnow, Dr Br. Meissner, and Dr H. Winckler have each contributed the text of one or two more. I shall give full references to these publications in my comments on the individual texts. In all nearly a hundred of this class of document are already more or less accurately known. They have often been translated and quoted or referred to \ but their many obscurities can only be cleared up by systematic examination andcomi)arison.

The issue of the Catalogue first made such systematic study possible. It has made known within narrow limits the extent of the existing material. To render the texts of these documents more widely available for students is the purpose of this work. The present volume contains the Cuneiform texts. The second volume, already far advanced towards completion, will contain a general introduction, detailed commentary, full index of proper names, a glossary, and lists or tables of prices, occupations, classes of goods, etc. To that volume reference must be made for all information I can give as to the literature of the subject and the meaning of the texts. By thus separating the auxiliary material from the texts, the perpetual inconvenience of reference from one page to another will be reduced to a minimum.

The same purpose is served though to a less extent by placing similar texts side by side. Instead of seeking parallel passages throughout the book, the reader will find them brought together as closely as possible. Obviously had all the tablets of each class been indicated in the Catalogue it would have been easy to copy each tablet and setid off the copy at once to the lithographer. Even to copy all first and then arrange them chronologically would have been comparatively easy especially as the dates are given so fully in the

chronological arrangement however loses much of its interest when no development has to be watched. Besides it would only have included a little more than half the tablets. To collect together all the transactions in which the same individual figured as principal would have had the interest attaching to personality but must have left a very large number of texts without any order. The interests of the student of the transactions themselves and of the phraseology in which the Assyrians expressed them demanded rather the toilsome process of sorting the texts into classes. In view of the ambiguity of the terms hitherto used and the difficulty both of reading the tablet and understanding the text it is too much to hope
My that the arrangement made will not need future revision.
chief desire is that it may be a step towards knowledge.

The ruling idea of the classification then has been to place first in each class those texts which exhibit most clearly the traits taken to be the class-characteristics. These need not be the most perfect considered either as tablets or texts. For all further details of the classes and their characteristics see vol. ii.
Some overlapping at least was unavoidable ; but I hope it will

lot prove a serious blemish. As an example of the necessarily ncomplete nature alike of the contents and their classification I may nstance the case of no. 714. The printing of the autography had eached the end of the class of " proclamations " when No. 4 of the AUorientalistische Literatur-Zeitung came into my hands. There on jage 70, Dr H. Winckler briefly stated that the " historical inscripion" K. 4467 of the Catalogue was really a Belehnungsurkunde. On ;opying it, the fragment was clearly seen to be part of no. 660 Bu. 91, 5, 9, 193) a text already printed. The text of the two joined "ragments is therefore given (out of its place) as no. 714.

:he real nature of the tablets in the Kouyunjik collection has been revealed by study. The present work may help to fix and define ideas of that nature so far as regards the tablets included.

In the register of tablets (p. xvii) will be found indications by tvhom each table.t has been previously published, but no notice is taken of mere references to their contents as for example Geo. Smith's

[juotations of their dates. In many cases my readings will be found to differ from those ilready published. It may be assumed that the difference is in:entional. I was not ignorant of the previous reading but gave it up because it seemed untenable. There is small pleasure in pointing 3ut mistakes in other people's work. Any one can find these errors for himself with as much trouble as it is worth. Possibly the previous copies were made hurriedly and never collated. The tablets themselves have undergone a systematic cleaning which in some cases has no doubt rendered perfectly legible what could only be matter of conjecture before. Further the comparison of a large number of similar texts gives one a great advantage over those who perhaps had seen only a single example. Lastly knowing by experience how difficult these tables are to copy I can only regret, never feel surprise at, any mistakes that are made.
Even great familiarity with the text has its dangers. One is apt, expecting some stock phrase or character in a certain connection, to

PREFACE, write it down even when the original scribe, with or without reason, wrote something else. This is especially likely in the case of homophonous characters. The Assyrian scribe seems sometimes to have taken a pride in shewing in how many different ways he could spell the same word. Moreover there are not only frequent variants, but many inaccuracies in the cuneiform texts. The scribe often impressed one wedge upon another in a way that defies counting.

Erasures are frequent, but sometimes the correction is merely written upon the word to be corrected. Unless then one knows, within a little, what ought to have been there such a passage can give no certain reading. Some tablets have blanks left as if for seal impressions. Occasionally these blanks are so narrow that no seal could possibly have been used. Elsewhere blank spaces have been left for the names of witnesses. Some tablets seem to have been rough drafts to be copied out ' fairly ' afterwards.

In the Cuneiform texts as lithographed few of these peculiarities appear. The forms of the characters are not intended to be exact reproductions. Photography alone can do justice to the niceties of script. The object of the work is not to give exercises in the decipherment of tablets but to present a fairly legible text. On the other hand it seemed a duty to give any peculiarities of orthography noticed, though these may equally well be slips on the part of the scribe. When a character seemed ambiguous the reading given is to be taken as- no more than an expression of opinion, and I indicate its doubtfulness by putting a row of dots over it thus

1 indicate a lacuna in the text in the same way by a row of dots in Hne with the text. Where no trace remains on the tablet to suggest a reading, but the usual phraseology leaves me no doubt as to what was originally there, I have restored the text without scruple. Such restorations are separated from the copied text by square brackets ; the arms of the brackets embracing the restoration and turning from the text.

These restorations frequently led to the identification of the proper fragment to join to the text. Everywhere I have avoided as much as possible "scratching" or "shading," preferring to leave out single wedges when they did not lead to a restoration. The text is thus left clear and clean for future restoration by conjecture or the identification of its 'join' or duplicate. A few 'joins' had already been made when the Catalogue was A printed. I am not aware by whom these were first noted.
Xlll systematic search however led to many more, and doubtless others
A will be recognised in time.
list of them so far is given on p. 552 of this volume. The joined tablet is always quoted by the registration mark of its first constituent taking the order of the entries in the

Catalogue. Thus K. 304 + K. 9804 is quoted as K. 304. In the register however a reference is given under both constituents to the number of the text. Thus both K. 304 and K. 9804 are given as no. 176. It will reassure the reader to know that fragments are not 'joined' at the British Museum, unless the actual fitting together of the pieces leaves no doubt of their real connection.

Sixty-eight of the ' contract ' tablets are said in the Catalogue to be written in the Babylonian character, and it is plausibly suggested of some that they did not come from Kouyunjik. Some are in archaic writing. They are of very various dates and differ entirely from the Assyrian contracts in style and personnel. As they seem to have no connection with the Assyrian contracts, they are not published in
list of their registration-marks is given on page xxiv.

The number of separate entries in the Catalogue under the heads of contracts, legal decisions and proclamations is 724. Some of these however are double or case tablets. The texts of all these are published in this volume with the exception of the Babylonian tablets referred to in the last paragraph and of five tablets written in

Aramaic (see page xxiv for list of their registration-marks). Making deductions for "joins" and adding a few texts from tablets entered under other heads we have in all 716 texts. Of these fully 600 are here published for the first time.

By far the greater number of the dated tablets belong to the 7th century B.C. and very many fall in the period after the latest date given by the existing copies of the Eponym Canon. Geo. Smith in The Assyrian Eponym Canon gave conjectural dates for several of these
Post-Canon Eponyms. These dates have not been accepted by
Strassmaier in his Alphabetisches Verzeic/miss, and Dr Bezold in his

Catalogue sometimes accei)ts, sometimes queries, sometimes gives other dates altogether. I am not aware that any reasons have been given anywhere for these dates. On the other hand the participation of the same persons in a long series of transactions at varying PostCanon dates ought to afford some grounds for a plausible order of
own attempt to fix this order will be submitted in the second volume. Meantime a register of dated documents following the order of the Canon will appear on page 559 ff. The
letters affixed to the Post-Canon Eponyms are used simply for convenience of reference and are by no means indications of their order. Thus Ep. B does not necessarily follow Ep. A.
We One definite conclusion may be deduced.
54 eponyms certainly occurring after B.C. 667. Excluding the four or five who may possibly be identified with others, this means that
Nineveh remained standing till after B.C. 613. It seems out of question to suppose that documents could be found in the palace at

Kouyunjik dated subsequent to the fall of Nineveh. Although this — date has been fixed from other considerations at B.C. 607 6, we have here for the first time native and original records bearing on the question.

This work was originally undertaken mainly for the sake of data to bear on the discussion of historical events and the fixing of dates. The interest of the general subject matter was so great however that

I often copied the whole text and at last copied them all. There is no need to say they are difficult to copy and to understand; testimony is unanimous on that point. It may be long before they are completely understood or some genius shall arise who shall see through all difficulties at a glance. Meantime much may be gathered even by one who has not the leisure nor perhaps the ability to become an Assyriologist. I only hope it will not be inferred from this preface that I know no more than I have said, nor that I have noticed nothing but what I have pointed out.

The side lights cast on history are numerous and to Cuneiform scholars will need no such pointing out. I may however be pardoned for drawing the attention of the general reader to the fact that in B.C. 694, presumably after the death of Sennacherib's eldest son Ashurnadinshum, or at least after his deportation to Elam, the crown-prince in
Nineveh was called Ardi-Belit or as has usually been read Arad-Belit.

Doubtless some will see in this name the original cuneiform of AradMalik and thence of Adrammelech. Dr J. A. Knudtzon in his Assyrische Gebete an den Sofinengott, Leipsic, 1893, published some texts (p. 211 flf.) giving the name of Esarhaddon's mother as Nika. In no. 645 the name is given as Nakia and as it seems the lady Zakute claims the same rank. Unless these are two names for the same person they must be those of two consorts of
Sennacherib. The lady Zakute is probably the Queen Mother who played such an important role in Esarhaddon's time and seems to have administered the government during his frequent absences

ibroad. She clearly survived Esarhaddon, for we find her along irilh Ashurbanipal, Shamashshumukin, ShamashdCirgatila and the lobles of Assyria issuing a proclamation to the people of the empire pparently announcing the accession of Ashurbanipal. There is an interesting instance of composition for manslaughter >r bloodmoney in no. 321. A slave is assigned hum dam'i, 'for )lood,' by the slayer, to the son of the slain man and has to be landed over before the funeral of the deceased ; otherwise the son nay take vengeance on the slayer by kiUing him. This is as far as I :now the first instance known in Assyrian documents of legal com- )Osition for homicide. Unfortunately the tablet is only a fragment, lowever one or two other points are clear. No other relative is lamed as having the right of exacting the blood penalty. The tenalty for subsequent repudiation of this settlement seems to have >een 10 maneh of silver to be paid to the treasury of Shamash, rhe date seems to be somewhere in the reign of Ashurbanipal.
